extracted.intended_audience: potential petitioners and their patent counsel / IP litigators considering filing IPRs or PGRs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and procedural standards for preparing, filing, and litigating inter partes reviews (IPRs) and post-grant reviews (PGRs) before the PTAB, including eligibility, timing, petition content, burdens, discovery, motions to amend, hearings, estoppel, settlement, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of IPRs and PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review ("IPR") or post-grant review ("PGR") is a proceeding designed to allow a Petitioner to attack the validity of one or more claims of an issued patent. These proceedings only examine validity and do not adjudicate infringement or award damages, injunctions, or other remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They were created by the American Invents Act (AIA). Use these proceedings as a faster, cheaper alternative to district court litigation when the goal is to attack validity only.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGR eligibility window and AIA-claim requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For PGRs, only patents with at least one AIA claim (priority date on or after March 16, 2013) are eligible. One must bring a PGR within nine months of issuance (or re-issuance) of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check claim priority dates and the nine-month post-issuance window carefully; missed windows foreclose PGR relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR eligibility and timing when AIA claims exist
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPRs, all patents are eligible and there is no general deadline for filing. However, if the target patent has at least one AIA claim, one must wait to file a Petition until the later of nine months after issuance (or re-issuance) or termination of any PGR on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate strategy across available post-grant options and watch for overlapping PGRs that can delay IPR filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of attacks allowed in IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPRs, the only attacks one can make are anticipation (35 U.S.C. § 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. § 103) based upon patents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to raise § 112 or § 101 grounds in an initial IPR petition (subject to exceptions for amended claims per Uniloc/precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of attacks allowed in PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: For PGRs, in addition to anticipation and obviousness attacks, one can also attack based upon lack of written description (35 U.S.C. § 112), indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. § 112), lack of enablement (35 U.S.C. § 112), and eligibility (35 U.S.C. § 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGRs permit broader validity challenges than IPRs; select forum based on the substantive grounds you intend to press.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court filing restriction (prior civil action)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to file an IPR or PGR attacking the validity of a patent, you (and any real party in interest) cannot have previously filed a civil action in district court challenging the validity of the same patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to initially attack validity in district court or before the PTAB because you generally cannot get 'two bites' at validity. Note: a civil action for declaratory judgment of noninfringement does not hinder PTAB challenges; filing a counterclaim for declaratory judgment of invalidity likewise does not bar subsequent PTAB petitions (see 35 U.S.C. §§ 315(a)(3), 325(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year deadline after service of complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have been served with a complaint for patent infringement in district court, you MUST file the petition within one year of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the one-year deadline seriously and leave time for unexpected issues; use one year from service even if the complaint had defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall timeline and major phases
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs and PGRs have two major phases: a pre-institution phase (which lasts up to six months) and a post-institution or 'trial' phase (which lasts up to twelve months, absent special circumstances), with the entire proceeding generally taking eighteen months or less from petition filing date to Final Written Decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan resources around these clocks; the brochure also details milestone clocks (e.g., Patent Owner optional Preliminary Response within 3 months; PTAB institution decision within ~3 months after Preliminary Response or waiver; post-institution briefing and discovery deadlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution thresholds (standard for instituting trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an IPR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the Petitioner will prevail as to at least one of the claims challenged (may encompass a 50/50 chance). For a PGR to be instituted, the Petition must demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged is unpatentable (greater than 50% chance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the petition to meet the appropriate standard: 'reasonable likelihood' for IPRs; 'more likely than not' for PGRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in IPRs and PGRs is 'preponderance of the evidence' whereas the burden of proof in district court and before the ITC is 'clear and convincing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the lighter PTAB standard strategically when validity challenges would face higher district-court burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director/panel discretion to institute
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the Petition meets the statutory thresholds, the panel has discretion on whether to institute a trial. Factors taken into account include: efficiency of the process, fundamental fairness, and whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office (see 35 U.S.C. §§ 314(a), 324(a); 315(d), 325(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate discretionary-denial arguments and avoid re-litigating arguments previously presented to the Office; consult the PTAB Consolidated Trial Practice Guide for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who is not the owner of the patent may file an IPR or PGR. (The Supreme Court clarified that the U.S. Government is not a 'person' for §311 and thus cannot bring an IPR or PGR.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm petitioner identity and ownership status before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and identification of real parties-in-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: No. The Petitioner and all real parties-in-interest must be identified. Failure to properly list all real parties-in-interest can be fatal to your attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct thorough corporate/contractual diligence to identify all RPIs and list them in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition scope and word limits; required petition contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition may only attack one patent. Petitions have word limits: 14,000 words for IPRs and 18,700 words for PGRs. The Petition must set forth: the grounds for standing, the claim(s) attacked, the statutory grounds for the attack, how the claims are to be construed, and how/why the construed claim is unpatentable. The Petition must also identify the real parties-in-interest, related matters, lead and back-up counsel, and service information. The Petition is typically supported by one or more declarations of technical experts and supporting exhibits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the petition to hit each required element within the word limits and attach supporting declarations/exhibits; any omission can jeopardize institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims in IPRs and PGRs are construed using the same claim construction standard that would be used to construe a claim in a civil action in district court, including 'construing the claim in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claims as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); see Phillips v. AWH Corp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claim construction arguments consistent with district-court Phillips-style constructions and cite prosecution history where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB clerical/procedural review upon filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a Petition is filed, the PTAB staff reviews the Petition for procedural compliance. The PTAB will either issue a Notice of Being Accorded a Filing Date (which starts the timeline) or a Notice informing the Petitioner of the deficiencies and setting a deadline for correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clerical compliance (format, fees, RPI disclosure, word limits) to obtain an unencumbered filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead counsel registration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead counsel in IPRs and PGRs must be registered to practice at the PTO. A district court attorney who is not registered may serve as back-up counsel if admitted pro hac vice; the PTAB generally permits such admission upon a showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm lead counsel PTO registration well before filing; plan for backup counsel admission if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing and post-institution fees and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO filing fee for an IPR is currently $19,000 (for up to 20 claims) and $22,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims). The PTO filing fee for a PGR is currently $20,000 and $27,500 for the post-institution fee (for up to 20 claims). Additional claims incur additional fees. If the petition is not instituted, the post-institution fee will be refunded upon request. In addition to filing fees, there will be significant fees associated with attorney time and expert witness compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for filing + post-institution fees and substantial attorney/expert costs; confirm current fee schedule before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-claim attacks allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petitioner may attack some or all of the claims of the patent on one or more grounds of unpatentability. The PTAB will decide whether the Petition meets the burden for at least one challenged claim. If that burden is met and the PTAB exercises its discretion in favor of the Petitioner, the trial will be instituted on all of the challenged claims and all of the alleged grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target claims strategically; you are not required to attack every claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Likely yes. Petitions are typically supported by at least one detailed declaration of a technical expert. The technical expert should have extensive experience in the subject matter, be technically proficient, able to set forth opinions and bases, and able to withstand deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain experts early; consider additional experts (e.g., economists) when addressing objective indicia of non-obviousness or rebutting Patent Owner evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Owner has the option to propose substitute claims via a Motion to Amend. Motions to Amend are only reached if a given claim is found unpatentable and the PTAB grants very few motions to amend. Rules (amended Jan 2021) state that the Patent Owner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the motion to amend complies' with statutory/regulatory requirements; and the Petitioner 'bears the burden of persuasion to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable.' The Board may exercise discretion to grant or deny only for reasons supported by readily identifiable and persuasive evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that motions to amend are difficult to win; if representing a Patent Owner, prepare persuasive evidence for compliance; if representing a Petitioner, prepare to attack substitute claims' patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing preparation and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Oral Hearing is one of few opportunities to interact with the APJ panel. Preparation is a must and requires in-depth familiarity with the record. Demonstrative exhibits are often submitted (which cannot include any new evidence). Litigants must be prepared to respond to interrogation by the Panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare demonstratives consistent with the record, rehearse direct responses to panel questions, and ensure witnesses/expert testimony already in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Written Decision contents and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Within three months of the Oral Hearing the panel issues its Final Written Decision, which addresses all bases and all claims raised in the Petition as well as patentability of any proposed amended claims. Final Written Decisions typically address claim construction (when necessary), weight given to experts’ opinions, fact-findings regarding scope and content of prior art, the Panel’s judgment on disputed evidence, and reasoning behind the Board’s conclusion as to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft the record and evidentiary support to influence claim construction, expert weight, and prior-art fact findings that will be recited in the Final Written Decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for rehearing may be filed within 30 days of the entry of a final decision. Requests for rehearing rarely succeed. Any such motion must specifically identify all matters the movant believes the Board misapprehended or overlooked, and indicate where in the record each matter was previously addressed in a motion, opposition, or reply (37 C.F.R. § 42.71(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise and point to the record when seeking rehearing; do not rely on rehearing as a likely corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to the Federal Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, in most instances. A Petitioner must have standing to file an appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. The Federal Circuit reviews Board decisions under the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires setting aside Board conclusions or findings that are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law,' or 'unsupported by substantial evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve issues in the record for appellate review and craft arguments cognizant of APA and substantial-evidence standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and the PTAB's right to continue
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may settle. But the PTAB has the right to step into the shoes of the Petitioner and proceed with the patentability analysis. The earlier in the process the proceeding is, the less likely the PTAB is to continue without both parties; the further along, the more likely the PTAB will finish its analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When negotiating settlements, consider PTAB's ability to proceed and the stage of the proceeding; early settlements more likely to produce dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel effects after Final Written Decision
rubrics_metrics.description: For an IPR or PGR that results in a Final Written Decision, a Petitioner (or real party-in-interest or privy) may not assert in district court or the ITC that any claim 'is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised' during the IPR or PGR (35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e)(2); 325(e)(2)). A Petitioner (and any real party-in-interest and privy) is estopped from requesting or maintaining a proceeding in the PTO with respect to a claim for which a Final Written Decision has issued on any ground that was raised or reasonably could have been raised in the IPR or PGR (35 U.S.C. §§ 315(e)(1), 325(e)(1); 37 C.F.R. § 42.73(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the risk of estoppel when deciding which grounds to present in the PTAB; incomplete presentation may preclude later arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery scope and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery is permitted but limited. Routine discovery includes: (1) production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony; (2) cross-examination of the other side’s declarants; and (3) relevant information inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding (PTAB Consolidated Trial Practice Guide). Additional discovery is allowed narrowly: for IPRs, if it furthers the 'interests of justice' (35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(2)); and for PGRs, where 'good cause' is shown and limited to evidence directly related to factual assertions advanced by either party (35 U.S.C. § 326(a)(5); 37 C.F.R. § 42.224).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build the record with admissible, cited exhibits; reserve broad or intrusive discovery requests for narrowly tailored, well-justified motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective order availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB has a default Protective Order. If either party wants a different Protective Order, there are procedures to get a different Order in place and the PTAB generally allows different Orders (provided the need is shown).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request alternative protective orders early and justify deviations from the default order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic rationale: speed, cost, and success rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability attacks before the PTAB have a high rate of success — approximately 60% of claims for which a trial has been instituted have been found unpatentable. Considering the high 'kill rate,' the speed, and the cost savings relative to district court proceedings, many find IPRs and PGRs attractive tools for removing patent obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use institutional statistics and timing/cost comparisons to advise clients on whether PTAB proceedings align with case goals and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition may only attack one patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition is a written document filed with the PTAB. It may only attack one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File separate petitions for different patents; coordinate multi-patent challenges carefully to manage fees and strategy.
